title: When the Will Turns
premise: Odile Oyelaran, the small-town coroner of Marrow Creek, has spent a lifetime keeping the town's dead organized and its secrets buried—until a missing woman's diary turns up in an estate sale, its entries continuing for three weeks after her disappearance. The diary belongs to Wren Halloway, who vanished in 1994, and its final pages describe a crime Odile recognizes: the unsolved death that once put Odile's own foster brother on trial. As Odile follows the diary's trail through alibis woven thirty years ago, they uncover that Wren faked her disappearance to survive a witness she couldn't name, and that the diary was her insurance policy. The killer is the town's beloved retired sheriff, who has been quietly eliminating everyone who remembers the original night; the climax comes when he comes for Odile in the records basement, and Wren—alive, watching, waiting thirty years for someone to read to the end—intervenes. The novel ends with the trial Odile never wanted, a town forced to grieve its myth, and Odile choosing at last to be seen, adopting Wren's stray daughter into the found family neither of them expected.
about_author: Rosalind Underhill is a former rural court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing small-town trials before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries from a farmhouse in the northern hills, where she keeps a documented archive of every storm that has crossed her valley since 1987.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Establishes Marrow Creek, the coroner's meticulous ledgers, and Odile's creed: every case closes. A routine estate-sale inventory brings a water-stained diary to their desk, sold from the house of a dead hoarder. The emotional beat is quiet pride about to be punctured.

chapters.title: Three Weeks Too Many
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The diary belongs to Wren Halloway, missing since 1994 and declared dead in absentia. Its entries continue nineteen days past her disappearance, ending mid-sentence. Odile, unsettled, checks the old file and finds pages missing. Beat: the first crack in Odile's certainty.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Doesn't Hold
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, with a flashback to Odile's foster childhood. Odile recalls the 1994 death of Denny Marsh and the trial of Odile's foster brother Teo, acquitted but exiled by the town. The diary's handwriting matches a note Teo once received. Beat: personal stakes ignite.

chapters.title: The Sheriff Who Never Left
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile visits retired Sheriff Amos Verrill, charming and helpful, who 'remembers nothing' about Wren but warns Odile against digging up old grief. That night, someone searches Odile's office. Beat: dread beneath civility.

chapters.title: Wren, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, 1994. Flashback chapters begin: Wren, a young court clerk, sees something the night Denny Marsh dies—something she tells one person only. She starts keeping the diary as protection. Beat: fear becoming method.

chapters.title: Teo Comes Home
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Teo returns for their foster mother's funeral, hard-edged and unwilling to discuss the trial. Odile shows him the diary; he goes white and leaves before dawn. Beat: betrayal-shaped love, old wounds reopened.

chapters.title: The Alibi Quilt
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile maps the 1994 alibis: five people, five seamless stories, too seamless. The diary's coded references suggest Wren interviewed each of them before vanishing. Beat: the puzzle takes shape; Odile's obsession deepens.

chapters.title: A Grave With No Body
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile exhumes the memorial plot bought for Wren—empty. Someone in town knew she never died. Odile suspects the estate-sale hoarder was Wren's silent ally. Beat: the missing woman becomes a living adversary.

chapters.title: Wren, Running
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, 1994–95. Wren realizes the person she told has passed her name to someone dangerous. She stages her disappearance with help from an unexpected source, leaving the diary behind deliberately. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of survival.

chapters.title: The Daughter Who Waits
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile tracks a woman named Ivy, Wren's daughter, raised by an aunt and told her mother abandoned her. Ivy is angry, guarded, and holds one postcard her mother never explained. Beat: found-family theme surfaces; Odile sees themselves in Ivy.

chapters.title: Second Death of Denny Marsh
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Reconstructing the 1994 night from the diary's fragments, Odile finds Denny's death wasn't what the trial claimed—he was killed elsewhere and moved. The coroner's original report was altered. Beat: the ground truth shifts.

chapters.title: Who Signed the Report
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The altered report bears the countersignature of Amos Verrill. Odile confronts him; he deflects with warmth, but that night Ivy's postcard is stolen from Odile's files. Beat: the hunter becomes the hunted.

chapters.title: Wren, Watching
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, present day. Wren has lived hidden nearby for decades, monitoring the diary's journey. She sees Verrill move against Odile and breaks her own rule of invisibility, leaving Odile a message only the diary's code can read. Beat: two watchers finally aligned.

chapters.title: The Code in the Margins
chapters.summary: Odile and Ivy's POV, alternating. Together they crack Wren's margin cipher: a name, a date, a location—the old grange hall, the night of the trial's verdict. Beat: partnership forming; grief and purpose braided together.

chapters.title: Teo's Silence Explained
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Teo finally confesses: he saw Verrill's deputy move the body and was made to believe his silence bought the family's safety. His alibi was manufactured for him. Beat: the foster brother is absolved; the true architecture of the lie exposed.

chapters.title: The Grange Hall
chapters.summary: Odile and Ivy's POV. They search the sealed grange hall and find Wren's hidden cache: photographs, the original autopsy page, and a letter naming Verrill. Verrill's truck pulls into the lot. Beat: trap closing from both directions.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Verrill's POV, first time. He explains, reasonably, monstrously, how he protected the town's peace by burying one death and then every witness. He offers Odile the same bargain offered to Teo. Beat: the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: The Records Basement
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Verrill traps Odile in the courthouse basement, cutting the lights. Odile stalls, recording on the coroner's dictaphone, as he confesses in the dark what he'll deny in daylight. Beat: terror and clarity; Odile stops being invisible.

chapters.title: Wren, Found
chapters.summary: Wren and Odile's POV. Wren intervenes—thirty years of preparation converging—and Verrill is taken into state custody. Mother and daughter meet in the courthouse hallway, furious and undone. Beat: climax resolves; reunion as wound and gift.

chapters.title: The Trial Begins
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The town fractures as the trial starts; old allies become strangers, and Odile testifies to what the ledger always knew. Teo sits in the gallery, finally a witness instead of a defendant. Beat: justice as slow, public, costly.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Verdict delivered, Odile walks the cemetery at dusk, speaking each name aloud, adding Wren's 'death' to the corrected record and striking it again. Beat: mourning the town's myth; Odile's creed revised—some names must be said, not filed.

chapters.title: When the Will Turns
chapters.summary: Odile and Ivy's POV, closing. Ivy moves into the room above Odile's office; Wren visits on her own terms, learning to be found. The diary's last unfinished entry gets a final line, written by all three. Beat: found family as the answer survival never expected.
